course_description:
The tourism and leisure industries are being increasingly fragmented into a series of niche or specialty travel forms of tourism that have emerged over recent years. Many tourists are now searching for novel and exciting types of experiences rather than opting for the traditional offerings cased in terms of passive engagement in industry driven and mass-produced, packaged products and services. The tourist of the 21st century is a savvy consumer who is motivated by a desire to indulge in new experiences across a range of diverse settings and has a desire for the authentic. Managers need to respond to these trends by understanding how to engage with tourists and to better design their services.

A special interest tourism (or niche tourism) market is a specific market segment, usually with a well-defined product that can be tailored to meet the needs and interests of the customer. Special interest tourism can be regarded as an alternative, almost the antithesis, to modern mass tourism, catering toﾠmore sophisticated needs and preferences of tourists. It is one of the most rapidly growingﾠsectors of tourism, with increasingﾠspecialisation of product offering in many destinations. Furthermore, special interest or niche tourism has also morphed into various sub-sections or "micro-niches" which will be investigated in this course. The tourism industry needs to quickly respond to create new markets that cater for quite particular tastes and preferences. In this situation, niche destinations are able to gain a competitive advantage in an expanded, overcrowded marketplace. This course investigates the history of special interest tourism, current developmentﾠand potential future developments, and has a significant practical element of designingﾠa special interest tour,ﾠin orderﾠto equip students for future careers in this increasingly important sector.

Sustainable Development Goals - UQ Business School is a proud supporter and Advanced Signatory of the United Nations Principles for Responsible Management Education (UN PRME) . As part of the largest global collaboration between business schools and the UN, the school emphasises its role in empowering students to drive societal transformation through the Sustainable Development Goals . The SDGs highlight that a thriving economy relies on a healthy environment, aiming to balance economic growth, social well-being, and environmental protection for a sustainable future.

Course Changes in Response to Previous Student Feedback

The course has moved from a blended learning format to a 1-hour in-person lecture and 2-hour tutorial each week to provide clearer structure, more face-to-face engagement, and stronger support for applied learning. The assessment suite has also been redesigned into a scaffolded sequence in which students experience a tour, analyse a market, design a real-world special interest tour, and defend their design through an interactive oral exam. These changes strengthen employability, AI literacy, client-focused learning, and assessment integrity while retaining the practical elements students value.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain the growth and development of special interest tourism over the past 30 years.
Analyse and compare the characteristics of a range of different types of tourism niche and micro-niche markets.
Evaluate market evidence from tourist, operator and destination perspectives to judge what matters for a named client and context.
Direct AI tools to gather and structure market evidence, then interrogate the output for sources, gaps and unfounded claims.
Design and justify a special interest tour for a named real-world client and community, working independently or in a team.

assessment_details.title: Special Interest Tourism Market Analysis (incl. tour reflection)
assessment_details.other_conditions: AI Required. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: A two-part assessment in which a low-stakes tour reflection contributes to a broader market analysis for The Brisbane Greeters. This assessment requires students to attend an in-person guided tour and analyse the market context for selected special interest tourism types. Students will use this evidence to identify opportunities, constraints, and implications for tour design. The task is completed in two connected parts. In Part A , students individually complete a short tour reflection based on their experience of participating in a guided tour during the current semester. The reflection requires students to critically consider the tourist experience, target market, tour theme, key moments, interpretation, and overall experience. Students are strongly encouraged to attend a Brisbane Greeters Walking Tour. These tours are free and take place daily at 10:00 am. Students can sign up here: https://www.brisbane.qld.gov.au/whats-on-in-brisbane/brisbane-greeter-tours Students may attend a different guided special interest tour; however, they must seek approval from the teaching team before completing the assessment to confirm that the tour is suitable. In Part B , students complete a market analysis for two types of special interest tourism markets relevant to The Brisbane Greeters. The analysis should draw on appropriate evidence to examine tourist demand, market characteristics, competitor or comparable experiences, destination opportunities, operational considerations, and relevant social, cultural, environmental, or commercial factors. Students are expected to use this analysis to identify what matters for the named client and context. The use of AI tools is an expected part of Part B. Students record how they directed AI tools to gather and structure market evidence, and how they checked the output for sources, gaps and unfounded claims, in a Decision and Evidence Log submitted as an appendix within the report. Together, Part A and Part B provide the evidence base for the later Special Interest Tour Design task. Students submit the report as a single document via Turnitin on Blackboard. assessment_details.other_conditions: Time limited. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: This assessment requires students to design a special interest micro-niche tour for The Brisbane Greeters and pitch it as a recorded video (5 minute duration maximum). The design must build directly on the A2 market analysis and justify key decisions using evidence about the target market, destination context, operator needs, and named client/community. Students may complete the task individually or in a team of up to three. The tour must be set in Brisbane, designed for a small group, include a clear special interest theme, and feature structured storytelling and one memorable WOW moment. Students submit: Recorded video pitch, The completed tour design template, A supporting promotional brochure. This is an AI-open task, but students must critically check AI output and ensure the final design and justification reflect their own reasoning. This assessment can be completed individually or in groups of 3 students (maximum). Further details and guidance will be provided on Blackboard and in class on selection of tour themes, locations, length of tour, etc. The template of design elements will be provided on Blackboard and explained in class. assessment_details.task_description: This live, in-person oral exam requires students to defend the reasoning behind their special interest tour design. Students respond to questions about their rationale behind their design, and how they made decisions when designing the tour. Questions are drawn from the video presentation submissions on how students weighed tourist, operator and destination evidence, developed their tour idea, identified what mattered for the community, and translated those judgements into a practical tour design. Students should be prepared to explain their reasoning in their own words, including the strengths and limits of their evidence and how they used or rejected AI-generated material. This is a secure, identity-verified assessment conducted without notes or electronic devices. For team submissions, each student is questioned individually to provide evidence of their own understanding and contribution. There is no written submission for this task.
